tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Mia avoids talking on the phone while she cycles through traffic.
The twins enjoy to bake cinnamon rolls on rainy Sundays.
After the match, the coach decided postponing the next training session.
Noah refused to share his notes before the chemistry quiz.
Lara promised delivering the costumes for the school play by Thursday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Mia avoids talking on the phone while she cycles through traffic.**

Avoid is one of the classic gerund verbs, so "avoids talking" matches the pattern exactly. The rest of the sentence — cycling through traffic — does not change what avoid requires. Mia is simply naming the activity she stays away from.

Keep this: avoid correctly pairs with the gerund talking.
**B) The twins enjoy to bake cinnamon rolls on rainy Sundays.**

Enjoy needs a gerund when its object is an activity, not a to-infinitive. Like and love can sound flexible in casual speech, but enjoy almost never takes to + verb here. Repair it to "enjoy baking cinnamon rolls."

**Tip:** If enjoy names an activity, use -ing.

Mark it wrong and prefer "enjoy baking cinnamon rolls."
**C) After the match, the coach decided postponing the next training session.**

Decide takes a to-infinitive, so the coach should have "decided to postpone," not "decided postponing." A bare gerund after decide is a frequent wrong choice because gerund verbs sit nearby in memory. The match-and-training context does not rewrite decide's pattern.

**Tip:** Decide / refuse / promise / plan lean toward to + base verb.

That complement fails — rewrite as "decided to postpone the next training session."
**D) Noah refused to share his notes before the chemistry quiz.**

Refuse correctly pairs with a to-infinitive: "refuse to share." The meaning is a willful no — he will not share the notes — and English packages that as refuse + to + verb. Nothing after the chemistry quiz changes the complement.

Accept the line: refuse wants to share, and that is what we have.
**E) Lara promised delivering the costumes for the school play by Thursday.**

Promise wants to + verb for a commitment: "promised to deliver the costumes," not "promised delivering." Commitment language after promise follows the same family as decide and refuse. The school-play deadline does not unlock a gerund after promise.

**Tip:** Promise patterns like decide — to + verb, not -ing.

Reject this; the clean commitment form is "promised to deliver the costumes."
tasks.solution_overview:
You are sorting five everyday sentences by whether the verb after avoid, enjoy, decide, refuse, or promise is in the form that verb actually wants.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Avoid and enjoy take a gerund (-ing). Decide, refuse, and promise take a to-infinitive. The trap is mixing those two camps: putting to after a gerund verb, or -ing after an infinitive verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the main verb that governs the second verb, then ask: is this an -ing verb or a to-verb? Match the complement to that list before you mark true or false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The hiking club is considering organising a dawn walk next month.
Sofia enjoys reading graphic novels on the train.
The family decided to camp beside the lake this weekend.
The barista refused accepting tips during the charity day.
Jamal promised to text when his flight landed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hiking club is considering organising a dawn walk next month.**

Consider takes a gerund, so "considering organising a dawn walk" is the right shape. The club is weighing an activity as an idea, which is exactly what consider + -ing expresses. The hiking context does not change the complement.

This is sound — consider takes organising as its gerund object.
**B) Sofia enjoys reading graphic novels on the train.**

Enjoy + gerund is the standard pattern: "enjoy reading graphic novels." Reading is the liked activity, so -ing is required. A to-infinitive after enjoy would be wrong here.

That works: enjoy + reading names the liked activity correctly.
**C) The family decided to camp beside the lake this weekend.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to camp beside the lake." They made a future plan, and decide packages plans with to + base verb. The weekend setting is just context.

Keep this: decided to camp packages the weekend plan the right way.
**D) The barista refused accepting tips during the charity day.**

Refuse needs a to-infinitive — "refused to accept tips," not "refused accepting." The charity-day setting does not change the grammar. Borrowing an -ing shape from avoid or enjoy is the usual misfire.

**Tip:** After refuse, swap a bare gerund for to + verb.

Mark it wrong and prefer "refused to accept tips."
**E) Jamal promised to text when his flight landed.**

Promise correctly takes a to-infinitive: "promised to text when his flight landed." That is a future commitment, which is the natural job of promise + to. The landed-flight clause is fine after the infinitive.

Accept the line: promise + to text is the standard commitment shape.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four of these lines already use the textbook complement; only one verb has crossed into the wrong pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Consider and enjoy want -ing. Decide, refuse, and promise want to + verb. Here the hiking club, Sofia, the family, and Jamal are fine; the barista's refuse line is the broken one.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for refuse first when the rest look polished — refuse is easy to contaminate with a gerund because avoid and enjoy sit nearby in your memory. Then confirm each remaining verb against its fixed list.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The librarian avoided to mention the overdue fines in front of the class.
Trainee chefs enjoy to practise knife skills on quiet mornings.
Management is considering to outsource the school canteen.
The band decided expanding their tour into two neighbouring towns.
The driver refused to open the boot without seeing ID.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The librarian avoided to mention the overdue fines in front of the class.**

Avoid needs -ing — "avoided mentioning the overdue fines," not "avoided to mention." Do not borrow the to-infinitive from decide or promise just because they sound similar. Mentioning the fines is the activity being steered clear of, so the gerund fits.

**Tip:** Avoid + gerund is fixed.

That fails here — rewrite as "avoided mentioning the overdue fines."
**B) Trainee chefs enjoy to practise knife skills on quiet mornings.**

Enjoy takes a gerund — "enjoy practising knife skills," not "enjoy to practise." Trainee chefs still follow the same grammar rule as anyone else. Practising is the liked activity, so -ing is required.

**Tip:** Enjoy / avoid / consider share the -ing pattern.

Reject this near-miss; prefer "enjoy practising knife skills."
**C) Management is considering to outsource the school canteen.**

Consider takes -ing — "considering outsourcing the school canteen," not "considering to outsource." If you can paraphrase as "the idea of …ing," you want a gerund. Consider to + verb is a frequent exam miss.

**Tip:** Reject consider to + verb; use consider + -ing.

Mark it wrong and prefer "considering outsourcing the school canteen."
**D) The band decided expanding their tour into two neighbouring towns.**

Decide needs to + verb — "decided to expand their tour," not "decided expanding." Decide never takes a bare gerund as its direct complement. The tour expansion is a future plan, which is classic decide + to.

**Tip:** Decide → to + base verb.

That gerund after decide fails — rewrite as "decided to expand their tour."
**E) The driver refused to open the boot without seeing ID.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to open the boot without seeing ID." Refusal language almost always pairs with to + base verb, and this line does it right. The ID condition sits after the infinitive without rewriting refuse's pattern.

Keep this: refuse to open is exactly how refusal + infinitive should look.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set is almost a wrong-pattern gallery: four sentences break the fixed complement, and only refuse survives cleanly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Avoid, enjoy, and consider must keep -ing; decide must keep to + verb. The only healthy line is refuse + to-infinitive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Flip every avoid/enjoy/consider error to a gerund and every decide error to to + verb. When refuse already has to, leave it alone.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We stopped to buy ice cream when we reached the pier.
Please stop to chew gum during the recital.
On the motorway they stopped talking and listened to the news.
She stopped to smoking after her doctor warned her.
He stopped typing when the fire alarm sounded.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We stopped to buy ice cream when we reached the pier.**

Stop + to-infinitive means they interrupted the journey in order to buy ice cream. That purpose reading fits the pier scene perfectly. The same verb with a gerund would mean quit buying, which is not the sense here.

**Tip:** Stop to = pause activity A in order to do B.

Accept the line: stop to buy correctly marks purpose after a pause.
**B) Please stop to chew gum during the recital.**

Here you want quit the habit of chewing gum during the recital — "stop chewing," not "stop to chew." Stop to chew would oddly mean pause something else in order to start chewing. The polite command is cessation of the same action.

**Tip:** Stop -ing = quit / no longer do that activity.

Mark it wrong and prefer "stop chewing gum during the recital."
**C) On the motorway they stopped talking and listened to the news.**

Stop + gerund means they quit talking and listened instead. On the motorway, the meaning is cessation of the same action, so -ing is the right form. A to-infinitive would wrongly read as pausing in order to talk.

That works — stop talking marks cessation of the same action.
**D) She stopped to smoking after her doctor warned her.**

Habit quitting needs the gerund alone — "stopped smoking," not "stopped to smoking." You cannot mix to and -ing in the same complement slot after stop. The doctor's warning frames a quit-habit sense, not a purpose pause.

**Trap:** "Stop to smoking" glues to onto an -ing form — that hybrid is never valid.

Reject this hybrid; the clean quit form is "stopped smoking."
**E) He stopped typing when the fire alarm sounded.**

Stop + gerund correctly means he quit typing when the fire alarm sounded. The typing itself ends; that is cessation, not purpose. Stop to type would mean pause something else in order to start typing.

Keep this: stop typing correctly ends the same activity, not a purpose pause.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stop is special: the form after it changes the meaning, so you are choosing a sense of the verb as well as a pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Stop + to-infinitive means pause in order to do something else. Stop + gerund means quit / no longer do that activity. Hybrids like "stop to smoking" are never valid.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask which sense the sentence needs — purpose after a pause, or cessation of the same action — then pick to or -ing to match. Reject any string that glues to onto an -ing form.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Athletes often avoid eating heavy meals right before a race.
My grandparents enjoy gardening in the late afternoon.
Have you considered joining the community choir?
Elena decided studying abroad for one semester.
The museum promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Athletes often avoid eating heavy meals right before a race.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid eating heavy meals right before a race." Health and habit advice often uses this pattern, and athletes are a natural context for it. A to-infinitive after avoid would break the fixed rule.

This is sound: avoid eating follows the fixed gerund pattern.
**B) My grandparents enjoy gardening in the late afternoon.**

Enjoy + gerund names a liked activity: "enjoy gardening in the late afternoon." Enjoy almost never takes to + verb in standard exam English. Gardening is simply the activity they like.

Keep this — enjoy gardening correctly names a liked activity.
**C) Have you considered joining the community choir?**

Consider + gerund is correct: "considered joining the community choir." Consider means think about doing something, which takes -ing. The polite question form does not unlock consider to.

Accept the line: consider + joining weighs the option with -ing.
**D) Elena decided studying abroad for one semester.**

Decide needs to + verb — "decided to study abroad," not "decided studying." Choose, refuse, and promise sit in the same to-infinitive family. A semester abroad is a future plan, so the infinitive is required.

**Tip:** Decide / choose / refuse / promise → to-infinitive.

That fails — rewrite as "decided to study abroad."
**E) The museum promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May.**

Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to reopen the sculpture wing in May." Commitments after promise use to + base verb. Public or personal promises both keep the to.

That pairing is sound — promise to reopen is the commitment form we want.
tasks.solution_overview:
Clean models for avoid, enjoy, consider, and promise sit beside one decide error that uses the wrong complement.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep the -ing trio (avoid, enjoy, consider) separate from the to-infinitive trio (decide, refuse, promise). Only Elena's decide line breaks the rule here.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Verify each governing verb against its list. When four look textbook-correct, still check decide/refuse/promise carefully for a smuggled gerund.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Tourists should avoid to swim near the rocks after dark.
Kids usually enjoy building sandcastles at low tide.
We are considering to rent bikes for the coastal path.
The jury refused to discuss the case outside the room.
Dad promised calling us as soon as the ferry docked.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Tourists should avoid to swim near the rocks after dark.**

Avoid takes -ing — "avoid swimming near the rocks," not "avoid to swim." Warnings with avoid always want the gerund. Do not borrow to from decide just because the sentence feels advisory.

**Tip:** Avoid + gerund is fixed; do not borrow to from decide.

Mark it wrong and prefer "avoid swimming near the rocks."
**B) Kids usually enjoy building sandcastles at low tide.**

Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoy building sandcastles at low tide." Building is the liked activity, so -ing is required. Enjoy to build would be the wrong camp.

Keep this: enjoy building correctly takes the gerund for the activity.
**C) We are considering to rent bikes for the coastal path.**

Consider takes -ing — "considering renting bikes," not "considering to rent." Consider to + verb is a frequent exam trap. If you can swap in "the idea of …ing," you want a gerund after consider.

**Tip:** If you can say "the idea of …ing," keep -ing after consider.

That consider to form fails — rewrite as "considering renting bikes."
**D) The jury refused to discuss the case outside the room.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to discuss the case outside the room." Refuse patterns with decide and promise, and this line keeps that to. The jury setting does not change the complement.

Accept the line: refuse to discuss matches the infinitive camp.
**E) Dad promised calling us as soon as the ferry docked.**

Promise needs to + verb — "promised to call us," not "promised calling." Promise + -ing is not standard for future commitments. The ferry-docked timing clause belongs after the infinitive.

**Tip:** Promise + to-infinitive for commitments.

Reject this; prefer "promised to call us."
tasks.solution_overview:
Two clean lines (enjoy, refuse) sit next to three pattern flips on avoid, consider, and promise.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch especially avoid/consider + to and promise + -ing — those are the crossed wires this set is fishing for. Enjoy and refuse already show the correct camps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Sort each verb into the -ing list or the to list, then check whether the written complement matches. Flip only the mismatches.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Runners stopped to stretch at the water station.
Please stop shouting; the neighbours can hear you.
We stopped for buying tickets at the kiosk.
She stopped to check the map because the path forked.
He stopped to listen music and missed the announcement.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Runners stopped to stretch at the water station.**

Stop to stretch means pause the run in order to stretch at the water station. Purpose after an interruption is exactly what stop + to-infinitive expresses. Stop stretching would mean quit stretching, which is the opposite sense.

**Tip:** Purpose after an interruption → stop + to-infinitive.

That works: stop to stretch marks purpose after interrupting the run.
**B) Please stop shouting; the neighbours can hear you.**

Stop shouting means quit the noisy behaviour. The neighbours can hear you, so the command is to cease that same action — gerund territory. Stop to shout would mean pause something else in order to start shouting.

Keep this — stop shouting correctly commands cessation of the same noise.
**C) We stopped for buying tickets at the kiosk.**

After stop, use to + verb for purpose, not for + -ing — "stopped to buy tickets," not "stopped for buying." For + -ing is not the purpose pattern you want here. The kiosk scene is a pause in order to buy.

**Trap:** "Stopped for buying" looks like purpose but the fixed purpose form is stop to + verb.

Mark it wrong and prefer "stopped to buy tickets at the kiosk."
**D) She stopped to check the map because the path forked.**

Stop to check means interrupt travel in order to check the map because the path forked. Reason or purpose after a pause takes the to-infinitive. Stop checking the map would mean quit checking, not pause to look.

Accept the line: stop to check is the purpose reading after the fork.
**E) He stopped to listen music and missed the announcement.**

As written, both form and preposition fail. You need either "stopped listening to music" (quit) or "stopped to listen to music" (pause in order to) — and listen always keeps to before music. The announcement-missed outcome also fits either repair once listen to is intact.

**Trap:** "Stop to listen music" drops listen's to and muddies the stop meaning choice.

Reject this; rewrite as "stopped listening to music" or "stopped to listen to music."
tasks.solution_overview:
Deepen the stop contrast and catch side traps like for + -ing and a broken listen phrase.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Meaning still decides between stop to (purpose) and stop -ing (cessation). Also reject "stopped for buying" and any listen phrase that drops its to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label each stop as purpose or quit first. Then check that purpose uses to + verb (not for + -ing) and that any listen pattern keeps listen to.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I avoid checking social media before breakfast.
They enjoy to watch documentaries about deep-sea life.
Have you considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks?
The committee decided to cancel the outdoor picnic.
She refused helping with the dishes until her homework was done.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I avoid checking social media before breakfast.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid checking social media before breakfast." That is a habit she tries not to do, which is classic avoid + -ing. Avoid to check would be the crossed pattern.

Keep this: avoid checking is the habit-steering gerund pattern.
**B) They enjoy to watch documentaries about deep-sea life.**

Enjoy needs -ing — "enjoy watching documentaries," not "enjoy to watch." Enjoy to + verb is almost never right in carefully marked English. Watching is the liked activity, so the gerund is required.

**Tip:** Enjoy to + verb is almost never right.

That fails here — rewrite as "enjoy watching documentaries."
**C) Have you considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks?**

Consider + gerund is correct: "considered changing your route to avoid the roadworks." Weighing an option takes -ing after consider. The nested avoid the roadworks phrase does not rewrite consider's complement.

This is sound — consider + changing weighs the option with -ing.
**D) The committee decided to cancel the outdoor picnic.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to cancel the outdoor picnic." Decisions about future actions take to + verb. The committee subject does not change the pattern.

Accept the line: decided to cancel packages the picnic decision correctly.
**E) She refused helping with the dishes until her homework was done.**

Refuse needs to + verb — "refused to help with the dishes," not "refused helping." Refuse + -ing is a classic false friend with avoid and enjoy. The homework condition does not unlock a gerund after refuse.

**Trap:** Refuse + -ing mimics avoid wrongly — flip it to to + verb.

Mark it wrong and prefer "refused to help with the dishes."
tasks.solution_overview:
A mix of clean avoid/consider/decide lines and two flips: enjoy with to, and refuse with -ing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Group the verbs by pattern before scoring. Avoid and consider stay with -ing; decide stays with to; enjoy to and refuse -ing are the traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Mark each governing verb's camp first, then check the complement. The two false lines are the ones that borrowed the other camp's form.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: After years of late nights, he finally stopped drinking energy drinks.
We stopped to ask a local which tram went to the museum.
They stopped to arguing when the teacher walked in.
She never enjoys waiting in long airport queues.
The cast promised rehearsing every evening until opening night.
tactical_explanations:
**A) After years of late nights, he finally stopped drinking energy drinks.**

Stop + gerund means quit the habit of drinking energy drinks after years of late nights. Habit change is the cessation reading, so -ing is correct. Stop to drink would mean pause in order to drink — not a quit story.

That works: stop drinking correctly marks habit cessation.
**B) We stopped to ask a local which tram went to the museum.**

Stop to ask means pause the journey in order to ask a local which tram went to the museum. Purpose after a pause takes stop + to. Stop asking would mean quit asking, which is not the travel sense.

Keep this — stop to ask marks purpose after pausing the journey.
**C) They stopped to arguing when the teacher walked in.**

Quit arguing needs the gerund alone — "stopped arguing," not "stopped to arguing." Do not glue to onto a gerund after stop. When the teacher walked in, the intended sense is cessation of arguing.

**Trap:** "Stopped to arguing" mixes the purpose to with an -ing form — never valid after stop.

Reject this hybrid; prefer "stopped arguing when the teacher walked in."
**D) She never enjoys waiting in long airport queues.**

Enjoy + gerund is correct even when negated: "never enjoys waiting in long airport queues." Negation does not change the enjoy + -ing pattern. Never does not unlock enjoy to.

Accept the line: enjoy waiting stays gerund even under never.
**E) The cast promised rehearsing every evening until opening night.**

Promise needs to + verb — "promised to rehearse every evening," not "promised rehearsing." Promise + -ing fails the commitment pattern. Opening-night urgency does not rewrite promise's complement.

**Trap:** Promise + -ing looks busy but commitments still want to + verb.

That commitment form fails — rewrite as "promised to rehearse every evening."
tasks.solution_overview:
Stop meaning splits again, plus a hybrid "to arguing" error and a promise trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep purpose (stop to) versus cessation (stop -ing) sharply separate. Also reject glued hybrids like "to arguing," and remember promise wants to + verb.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each stop line, name the intended sense first. Then check enjoy's gerund and promise's infinitive independently.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Passengers should avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases.
Would you consider to volunteer at the food bank this winter?
The captain decided to turn back because of the fog.
My brother refuses admitting he lost the house keys.
Aunt Priya enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Passengers should avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoid blocking the aisle with large suitcases." Public notices often use avoid + -ing, and this one is textbook. Avoid to block would be the wrong camp.

Keep this: avoid blocking correctly uses the public-notice gerund.
**B) Would you consider to volunteer at the food bank this winter?**

Consider takes -ing — "consider volunteering at the food bank," not "consider to volunteer." Consider to is a frequent trap in polite offers. Would you consider still wants the gerund.

**Trap:** Consider to + verb is a common exam near-miss; rewrite with -ing.

Mark it wrong and prefer "consider volunteering at the food bank."
**C) The captain decided to turn back because of the fog.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to turn back because of the fog." Sudden decisions still take to + verb. The fog reason clause does not change decide's pattern.

That pairing is sound — decided to turn back takes the infinitive.
**D) My brother refuses admitting he lost the house keys.**

Refuse needs to + verb — "refuses to admit he lost the house keys," not "refuses admitting." Refuse + -ing wrongly mimics avoid. Admitting the loss is still a refuse + to situation.

**Trap:** Refuse + -ing borrows avoid's shape — flip to to + verb.

That fails — rewrite as "refuses to admit he lost the house keys."
**E) Aunt Priya enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family.**

Enjoy + gerund is correct: "enjoys knitting scarves for the whole family." Hobby verbs after enjoy always take -ing. Enjoy to knit would be wrong in exam English.

Accept the line: enjoy knitting correctly names the hobby with -ing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Three solid models sit beside two crossed patterns: consider with to, and refuse with -ing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Sort each verb into the -ing list (avoid, consider, enjoy) or the to list (decide, refuse) before you answer. The false lines are the ones that swapped camps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm avoid/enjoy/decide first as clean anchors, then repair consider to → -ing and refuse -ing → to + verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We decided not to climb the ridge after the weather warning.
She avoids not to sit near the speakers at concerts.
They refused not to apologise, even though everyone expected it.
He promised not to spoil the ending of the film.
I enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We decided not to climb the ridge after the weather warning.**

Decide + not + to-infinitive is the correct negation: "decided not to climb the ridge." You negate the infinitive with not before to, not by switching to a gerund. The weather warning explains why, without changing the pattern.

Keep this: decided not to climb correctly negates the infinitive.
**B) She avoids not to sit near the speakers at concerts.**

Avoid already means "not do"; use "avoids sitting near the speakers," not "avoids not to sit." Do not stack an extra not + to onto avoid. The concert setting still wants plain avoid + -ing.

**Trap:** Avoid + not to double-negates a verb that already means "stay away from."

Reject this stacked negation; prefer "avoids sitting near the speakers."
**C) They refused not to apologise, even though everyone expected it.**

The intended sense is almost always "refused to apologise" (would not apologise). "Refused not to apologise" is a double-negative mess unless you truly mean they insisted on apologising. Everyone expected an apology, so the natural reading fails as written.

**Trap:** Refused not to usually muddles refuse to; put not only when you truly mean "refuse to not do X."

Mark it wrong and prefer "refused to apologise" (unless insistence is truly meant).
**D) He promised not to spoil the ending of the film.**

Promise + not + to-infinitive is correct: "promised not to spoil the ending." Negation sits before to in the infinitive pattern, same family as decide. The film context does not change the placement of not.

Accept the line: promised not to spoil places not before to.
**E) I enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays.**

Enjoy + gerund works with negation inside the activity: "enjoy not waking up to an alarm on Sundays." Enjoy still wants -ing even when the activity is a negative state. Not belongs with the gerund phrase, not with a to-infinitive after enjoy.

That works — enjoy not waking keeps the gerund under internal negation.
tasks.solution_overview:
Negation tests the same fixed patterns: not to after decide/promise, plain -ing after avoid/enjoy, and careful handling of refuse.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Decide and promise negate with not before to. Avoid already means "not do," so it wants plain -ing, not a stacked not to. Refuse not to is usually a muddled double negation when the speaker meant refused to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Find the governing verb, apply its usual complement, then place not only where that pattern allows — before to for infinitives, inside the gerund phrase for enjoy, and nowhere extra after avoid.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Midway through the hike we stopped drinking from the stream and switched to bottled water.
Midway through the hike we stopped to drink from our bottles.
The guide stopped us from approaching the cliff edge.
Please stop to interrupting the speaker with side comments.
They stopped singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Midway through the hike we stopped drinking from the stream and switched to bottled water.**

Stop + gerund means quit the activity of drinking from the stream and switch to bottled water. The same action ends, so -ing is correct. Stop to drink would mean pause hiking in order to drink — a different sense.

This is sound: stop drinking marks cessation of the same stream-drinking.
**B) Midway through the hike we stopped to drink from our bottles.**

Stop to drink means pause walking in order to drink from our bottles. The purpose of the pause is the drink, so to-infinitive is correct. Stop drinking would mean quit drinking, not pause to drink.

Keep this — stop to drink marks the purpose of the walking pause.
**C) The guide stopped us from approaching the cliff edge.**

Stop someone from + -ing is a related but valid pattern: the guide prevented them from approaching the cliff edge. That is not the same as stop to or bare stop -ing, but it is grammatical. The object us + from + approaching carries the prevent sense.

**Tip:** Stop + object + from + -ing = prevent.

Accept the line: stop us from approaching correctly marks prevention.
**D) Please stop to interrupting the speaker with side comments.**

Quit interrupting needs "stop interrupting," not "stop to interrupting." Never attach to directly to an -ing form after stop. The speaker-command sense is cessation of the same annoying act.

**Trap:** "Stop to interrupting" is the hybrid purpose-marker glued onto a gerund.

That hybrid fails — rewrite as "stop interrupting the speaker."
**E) They stopped singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand.**

Stop + gerund means they quit singing as soon as the conductor raised her hand. Instant cessation of the same action takes -ing. Stop to sing would mean pause in order to start singing.

That works: stop singing correctly marks instant cessation.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pair stop to / stop -ing with the prevent pattern stop someone from -ing, and reject the hybrid "to interrupting."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Same action ending → stop + -ing. Purpose of a pause → stop + to. Preventing someone → stop + object + from + -ing. Never write stop to + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the intended meaning of stop in each line. Then match the structure: gerund, to-infinitive, or object + from + -ing — and kill the hybrid.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Having considered moving house, they decided to stay another year.
She enjoys to be the first to arrive at rehearsals.
We avoided discussing politics at the family dinner.
He refused being photographed without his consent.
The mayor promised to fund the new skate park next spring.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Having considered moving house, they decided to stay another year.**

Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive both follow their fixed patterns in one sentence: having considered moving, they decided to stay. Different verbs keep their own complements; one correct pattern does not rewrite its neighbour.

**Tip:** Different verbs in the same sentence can still keep their own complements.

Keep this: considered moving and decided to stay each match their own verb.
**B) She enjoys to be the first to arrive at rehearsals.**

Enjoy needs -ing — "enjoys being the first to arrive," not "enjoys to be." Enjoy + being / doing, never enjoy to be in this sense. Being first is the liked state, so the gerund is required.

**Trap:** Enjoy to be looks polished but enjoy still wants being / doing.

Mark it wrong and prefer "enjoys being the first to arrive."
**C) We avoided discussing politics at the family dinner.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided discussing politics at the family dinner." Sensitive topics often pair with avoid + -ing. Avoid to discuss would be the wrong camp.

Accept the line: avoid discussing correctly takes the gerund.
**D) He refused being photographed without his consent.**

Refuse needs to + verb — "refused to be photographed without his consent," not "refused being." Passive infinitives still follow refuse + to. Being photographed after refuse wrongly borrows the gerund camp.

**Trap:** Passive voice does not unlock refuse + -ing — keep refuse to be + past participle.

That passive after refuse fails — rewrite as "refused to be photographed without his consent."
**E) The mayor promised to fund the new skate park next spring.**

Promise + to-infinitive is correct: "promised to fund the new skate park next spring." Public commitments use promise + to. A gerund after promise would break the commitment pattern.

This is sound — promised to fund is the commitment infinitive.
tasks.solution_overview:
Stacked verbs, a passive after refuse, and an enjoy trap — track each verb's complement independently.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Consider + -ing and decide + to can share one sentence without rewriting each other. Enjoy still wants -ing (including being). Refuse needs to even before a passive infinitive. Promise keeps to.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline every verb that governs another verb form, then apply that verb's own rule. Do not let one correct pattern contaminate its neighbour.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I never stop to wonder how the magician hid the coin.
I never stop wondering how the magician hid the coin.
Doctors advised him to stop to smoke immediately.
They decided against postponing the wedding.
She is considering whether to accept the internship offer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I never stop to wonder how the magician hid the coin.**

The intended idiom is continuous curiosity — "never stop wondering" (gerund), not pause-in-order-to wonder. Stop to wonder would mean interrupt something else so you can wonder, which is not the usual reading. I never stop + -ing means keep doing that all the time.

**Trap:** Never stop to + verb sounds close to the idiom but the fixed phrase wants never stop + -ing.

Reject this near-miss; the idiom wants "never stop wondering."
**B) I never stop wondering how the magician hid the coin.**

Never stop + gerund correctly means the wondering continues without pause. Idiomatic "can't/never stop -ing" always wants the gerund. The magician clause is simply the object of wondering.

Keep this: never stop wondering correctly marks continuous curiosity.
**C) Doctors advised him to stop to smoke immediately.**

Quit smoking needs "stop smoking"; "stop to smoke" would mean pause something else in order to smoke — the opposite of medical advice to quit. Doctors advised him to stop smoking immediately.

**Trap:** Stop to smoke after quit-advice flips the intended cease sense into purpose.

That purpose reading fails the quit advice — rewrite as "stop smoking immediately."
**D) They decided against postponing the wedding.**

Decide against + gerund is a valid related pattern: "decided against postponing the wedding." You can also say decide to + verb; against + -ing is the negative sibling. Here postponing sits under against, not as decide's bare complement.

**Tip:** Decide to + verb OR decide against + -ing.

Accept the line: decide against postponing is a legal against + -ing frame.
**E) She is considering whether to accept the internship offer.**

Consider whether + to-infinitive is grammatical when whether introduces the option: "considering whether to accept." Bare consider + verb still wants -ing; the whether-clause changes the frame. The internship offer is the embedded choice, not a bare consider + verb slot.

**Tip:** Bare consider + verb → -ing; consider whether → to is fine.

That works — considering whether to accept uses the wh- + to frame cleanly.
tasks.solution_overview:
Idioms and near-neighbours: never stop -ing, stop smoking versus stop to smoke, decide against -ing, and consider whether to.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Never stop -ing" means keep doing something. Medical quit advice wants stop + -ing, not stop to. Decide against + gerund and consider whether + to are valid alternatives to the basic patterns.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read for idiom and structure, not just the first verb. Ask whether stop means cease or purpose, and whether decide/consider are using a legal alternative frame.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Rather than argue, they decided to sleep on the problem.
She avoids to be seen wearing the same outfit twice.
We enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues.
He refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa.
The club promised arranging free coaching for beginners.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Rather than argue, they decided to sleep on the problem.**

Decide + to-infinitive is correct: "decided to sleep on the problem." The opener "Rather than argue" does not change decide's to-pattern. Sleeping on the problem is the planned action packaged with to.

Keep this: decided to sleep correctly takes the to-infinitive.
**B) She avoids to be seen wearing the same outfit twice.**

Avoid needs -ing — "avoids being seen wearing the same outfit twice," not "avoids to be seen." Passive gerunds still follow avoid + -ing. Being seen is the state she steers clear of.

**Trap:** Passive "to be seen" after avoid is a polished near-miss; keep avoid + being.

Mark it wrong and prefer "avoids being seen wearing the same outfit twice."
**C) We enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues.**

Enjoy + gerund (passive) is correct: "enjoy being invited to their rooftop barbecues." Enjoy + being + past participle is a common natural pattern. Active or passive form does not unlock enjoy to.

Accept the line: enjoy being invited keeps the gerund even in the passive.
**D) He refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct: "refused to let the puppy sleep on the sofa." Refuse to let / refuse to allow keep the to. The puppy clause is the object of let, not a gerund after refuse.

This is sound — refused to let matches refuse + to.
**E) The club promised arranging free coaching for beginners.**

Promise needs to + verb — "promised to arrange free coaching," not "promised arranging." Promise + -ing is still wrong even with a kind offer. Beginners' coaching does not rewrite the commitment pattern.

**Trap:** Kind offers after promise still want to + verb, not a bare gerund.

That fails — rewrite as "promised to arrange free coaching."
tasks.solution_overview:
Passive gerunds after avoid/enjoy and a promise error — form (active/passive) does not rewrite the verb's complement rule.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Decide and refuse keep to. Avoid and enjoy keep -ing, including being + past participle. Promise still cannot take a bare gerund.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ignore active versus passive cosmetics and ask only what the governing verb demands. Repair avoid to be → being, and promise arranging → to arrange.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: What made them stop to check the tyre pressure was a strange vibration.
What made them stop checking their phones was the no-device rule.
Investors are considering selling a small stake in the start-up.
She decided that postponing the trip would be wiser.
He enjoys when friends drop by without calling first.
tactical_explanations:
**A) What made them stop to check the tyre pressure was a strange vibration.**

Stop to check means pause driving in order to check the tyre pressure after a strange vibration. The cleft "what made them…" still keeps stop's meaning split intact. Purpose of the pause is what the to-infinitive marks.

That works: stop to check marks purpose inside the cleft.
**B) What made them stop checking their phones was the no-device rule.**

Stop checking means quit the phone-checking habit because of the no-device rule. Same cleft frame, opposite stop pattern — meaning decides. The gerund marks cessation of the same action.

Keep this — stop checking marks cessation inside the same cleft frame.
**C) Investors are considering selling a small stake in the start-up.**

Consider + gerund is correct: "considering selling a small stake in the start-up." Even in money contexts, consider still wants -ing. Consider to sell would be the crossed camp.

Accept the line: considering selling correctly takes the gerund.
**D) She decided that postponing the trip would be wiser.**

Decide that + clause is grammatical; the gerund postponing is the subject of the that-clause, not decide's complement. Decide to + verb OR decide that + clause — both work. Here that carries the content of the decision.

**Tip:** Decide to + verb OR decide that + clause — both work.

This is sound: decide that + clause is a legal alternative to decide to.
**E) He enjoys when friends drop by without calling first.**

Enjoy can take a when-clause as its object; no verb-complement conflict arises. Enjoy + noun/gerund/clause are fine — but not enjoy to + verb. Friends dropping by is a situation clause, not an activity infinitive.

**Tip:** Enjoy + noun/gerund/clause — but not enjoy to + verb.

Keep this: enjoy when… correctly takes a situation clause as object.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five are sound once you separate stop's two meanings and allow decide that / enjoy when as alternative structures.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Cleft frames do not rewrite stop to versus stop -ing. Consider still wants -ing. Decide that + clause and enjoy + when-clause are grammatical alternatives to decide to / enjoy + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check stop by meaning first, then accept legal clause objects after decide and enjoy. Do not force every verb into only one complement shape.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Far from avoiding to answer, she volunteered the awkward detail first.
They kept promising finishing the mural before the festival.
Only after refusing to compromise did the two sides walk out.
Having enjoyed to sail as children, they booked a dinghy again.
Stop to pretend you did not hear the question.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Far from avoiding to answer, she volunteered the awkward detail first.**

Avoid still needs -ing — "avoiding answering," not "avoiding to answer." Far from + -ing does not license avoid + to. Strip the wrapper and the bare rule is still avoid + gerund.

**Trap:** Far from… does not unlock avoid to; the complement rule survives the wrapper.

Mark it wrong and prefer "avoiding answering."
**B) They kept promising finishing the mural before the festival.**

Promise needs to + verb — "promising to finish the mural," not "promising finishing." Keep / start do not change promise's to-pattern. Kept promising still embeds finish as an infinitive.

**Trap:** Keep -ing around promise still leaves promise wanting to + verb.

That fails inside keep promising — rewrite as "promising to finish the mural."
**C) Only after refusing to compromise did the two sides walk out.**

Refuse + to-infinitive is correct inside the inversion: "refusing to compromise." Inversion and emphasis leave the refuse + to pattern intact. Only after… did… is wrapper, not a new complement rule.

Accept the line: refusing to compromise keeps refuse + to under inversion.
**D) Having enjoyed to sail as children, they booked a dinghy again.**

Enjoy needs -ing — "enjoyed sailing as children," not "enjoyed to sail." The perfect participle having enjoyed still takes -ing. Childhood hobby language does not unlock enjoy to.

**Trap:** Having enjoyed still takes -ing; the participle wrapper does not license to.

Reject this; prefer "Having enjoyed sailing as children."
**E) Stop to pretend you did not hear the question.**

Quit pretending needs "stop pretending," not "stop to pretend" (which would mean pause in order to pretend). Commands to quit an act use stop + -ing. You did not hear the question is the act being told to cease.

**Trap:** Stop to pretend reads as purpose; quit-commands need stop + -ing.

That purpose reading fails the quit command — rewrite as "Stop pretending you did not hear the question."
tasks.solution_overview:
Hard wrappers (far from, keep -ing, inversion, having -ed) still cannot rewrite avoid, enjoy, promise, or stop. Only refuse to survives cleanly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Far from + -ing does not license avoid + to. Keep promising still needs to finish. Inversion leaves refuse + to intact. Having enjoyed still takes -ing. Quit-commands need stop + -ing, not stop to pretend.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip the fancy wrapper mentally, apply the bare verb's complement rule, then put the wrapper back. Only the refuse line already matches.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She stopped to mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath.
If you stop meaning what you say, people stop trusting you.
We are still considering how to phrase the apology.
He decided on renting the attic flat above the bakery.
They refused their friends' offer of driving them home.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She stopped to mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath.**

Stop to mean is not English for "intend." Use something like "She did not mean that she was leaving; she simply paused for breath." Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action — mean is not one.

**Trap:** Stop to + verb only works for real purpose actions; "mean" fails that test.

Reject this; repair the sense — e.g. "She did not mean that she was leaving…"
**B) If you stop meaning what you say, people stop trusting you.**

Stop + gerund twice: quit meaning what you say / quit trusting you. Parallel stop + -ing structures keep the "cease" sense cleanly. The conditional frame does not rewrite stop's cessation pattern.

Keep this: stop meaning / stop trusting correctly mark parallel cessation.
**C) We are still considering how to phrase the apology.**

Consider + how + to-infinitive is fine when how introduces the method: "considering how to phrase the apology." Consider + -ing OR consider + wh-word + to both work. Here how to phrase is the embedded method question.

**Tip:** Consider + -ing OR consider + wh-word + to.

Accept the line: considering how to phrase uses the wh- + to method frame.
**D) He decided on renting the attic flat above the bakery.**

Decide on + gerund/noun is a valid alternative to decide to + verb: "decided on renting the attic flat." Decide to go OR decide on going — both grammatical. On renting carries the choice as a prepositional object.

**Tip:** Decide to go OR decide on going — both grammatical.

That works — decided on renting is a legal decide on + -ing alternative.
**E) They refused their friends' offer of driving them home.**

Refuse can take a noun object ("refused their friends' offer"); the of + -ing belongs to offer, not to refuse. Refuse + noun and refuse + to + verb are both correct. Do not force a to-infinitive when the object is already a noun phrase.

**Tip:** Refuse + noun and refuse + to + verb are both correct.

This is sound: refused their friends' offer correctly takes a noun object.
tasks.solution_overview:
Edge grammar: impossible stop to mean, parallel stop -ing, consider how to, decide on -ing, and refuse + noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Stop to only works when the infinitive is a real purpose action — "mean" is not one. Parallel stop + -ing keeps the cease sense. Consider how to, decide on -ing, and refuse + noun are all legal alternatives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Look past the first verb when the complement sits elsewhere (offer of driving). Reject nonsense purpose infinitives, and accept decide on / consider how / refuse + noun when they appear.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided interrupting the poet mid-line.
Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided to interrupt the poet mid-line.
They promised that they would water the plants while we were away.
He enjoys that his sister always remembers his birthday.
We stopped short of promising to host the entire reunion.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided interrupting the poet mid-line.**

Avoid + gerund is correct: "avoided interrupting the poet mid-line." Fronted participle clauses (Not wishing to appear rude) do not change avoid's -ing rule. Interrupting is still the activity she steers clear of.

Keep this: avoided interrupting correctly keeps avoid + -ing after the fronted clause.
**B) Not wishing to appear rude, she avoided to interrupt the poet mid-line.**

Same sentence with the wrong complement — avoid needs -ing, not to. Compare the pair; only the gerund version works. Not wishing to appear rude does not license avoid to interrupt.

**Trap:** The fronted clause makes avoid to look elegant, but avoid still wants -ing.

Mark it wrong and prefer "avoided interrupting the poet mid-line."
**C) They promised that they would water the plants while we were away.**

Promise that + clause is a valid alternative to promise to + verb: "promised that they would water the plants." Promise to water OR promise that we will water. The that-clause carries the commitment content.

**Tip:** Promise to water OR promise that we will water.

Accept the line: promised that… would water is a legal clause alternative.
**D) He enjoys that his sister always remembers his birthday.**

Enjoy that + clause is acceptable; the that-clause is the object of enjoy. Enjoy + -ing for activities; enjoy that for facts or situations. His sister remembering the birthday is a fact/situation, not an infinitive activity.

**Tip:** Enjoy + -ing for activities; enjoy that for facts/situations.

That works — enjoy that… correctly takes a fact/situation clause.
**E) We stopped short of promising to host the entire reunion.**

Stop short of + -ing is an idiom meaning "almost but not quite"; promising keeps its own to inside the gerund phrase. Idioms can nest: stop short of + gerund, and inside it promise + to. Hosting the reunion is the nearly-made promise, not a bare stop to host.

**Tip:** Idioms can nest stop short of + gerund with promise + to inside.

This is sound: stopped short of promising to host nests both patterns legally.
tasks.solution_overview:
Minimal pairs, that-clause alternatives, and the idiom stop short of -ing. Confirm which structure is actually complementing which verb.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Avoid keeps -ing even after a fronted participle clause; the to version is the false twin. Promise that and enjoy that are valid clause objects. Stop short of + -ing nests another verb's complement inside an idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Compare near-identical lines first. Then check whether that-clauses or idioms are carrying the object, so you do not over-apply the basic to/-ing rule to the wrong verb.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait for clearer skies.
She cannot help enjoying to win, even in friendly matches.
Whatever they refuse to discuss in public, they still avoid lying to each other.
To stop to worry is not the same as to stop worrying.
Only those who promise delivering results on time keep their places on the team.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait for clearer skies.**

Consider + gerund and decide + to-infinitive are both correct inside a conditional: had they considered postponing, they might have decided to wait. Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement.

**Tip:** Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement.

Keep this: considered postponing and decided to wait each keep their own rule.
**B) She cannot help enjoying to win, even in friendly matches.**

Enjoy needs -ing — "enjoying winning," not "enjoying to win." Cannot help + -ing is itself a gerund pattern and does not license enjoy to. Nested -ing still leaves enjoy wanting a gerund object.

**Trap:** Cannot help enjoying does not unlock enjoy to; keep enjoying winning.

That fails — rewrite as "enjoying winning."
**C) Whatever they refuse to discuss in public, they still avoid lying to each other.**

Refuse + to and avoid + -ing are both correct in parallel clauses: whatever they refuse to discuss, they still avoid lying. Different verbs, different complements — both can be right at once.

Accept the line: refuse to discuss and avoid lying both match their verbs.
**D) To stop to worry is not the same as to stop worrying.**

The contrast is precisely the teaching point: stop to worry is not the same as stop worrying. Infinitive subjects can showcase the stop meaning split cleanly, and both halves are grammatical as a contrast. Purpose pause versus cessation sit side by side on purpose.

**Tip:** Infinitive subjects can showcase the stop meaning split cleanly.

That pairing is sound — the stop to / stop -ing contrast teaches the split cleanly.
**E) Only those who promise delivering results on time keep their places on the team.**

Promise needs to + verb — "promise to deliver results on time," not "promise delivering." Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing. Those who… still wrap a complement that must match promise.

**Trap:** Relative-clause wrappers do not unlock promise + -ing.

Mark it wrong and prefer "promise to deliver results on time."
tasks.solution_overview:
Final stress test: stacked patterns, cannot help + enjoy, parallel refuse/avoid, the stop meaning contrast as subject, and a last promise trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Complex syntax still respects each verb's fixed complement. Cannot help + -ing does not license enjoy to. Refuse to and avoid -ing can both be right at once. Infinitive subjects can showcase stop to versus stop -ing. Relative clauses do not unlock promise + -ing.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Parse each governing verb on its own, even inside conditionals, clefts, and relative clauses. Mark true only when every stacked pattern is legal; the enjoy to and promise -ing lines fail.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
